newsitem.title: UK: Netherlands may hold large stocks of hidden copper.
newsitem.headline: Netherlands may hold large stocks of hidden copper.

text.p: Between 1990 and 1995 receipts of refined copper in to bonded warehouses in the Netherlands have exceeded deliveries out by more than 500,000 tonnes, while the London Metal Exchange (LME) has only reported a small decrease in inventory, the World Bureau of Metal Statistics (WBMS) said.
In its latest monthly issue of World Metal Statistics the WBMS queried whether the difference of 588,000 tonnes could be unrecorded stocks held in Rotterdam bonded warehouses.
"If we look at the numbers around 600,000 tonnes of copper appears to have gone into warehouses and not come out," Lloyd Davies, WBMS General Manager said.
The analysis is based on data from the Dutch Central Bureau of Statistics and the LME, and no such statistical anomaly exists in nickel, for example, the WBMS noted.
With nickel the bulk of metal is refined to meet LME requirements, so it might be expected to show up in LME stocks.

"For refined copper, however, all the material coming from the former Soviet Union (FSU) - more than one million tonnes between 1991 to 1994, accounting for over half of total receipts - did not meet such a specification and could never therefore be counted in reported LME stocks," the WBMS said.
"This is possibly the strongest argument in favour of such non-LME stocks," it said.
The pattern of deliveries also suggests China was the destination of a large volume of refined copper leaving the Netherlands in 1993 when there was no overall change in LME stocks.

Other factors behind the discrepancy could be that some of the data refers to copper alloy ingots, while there may be differences in the timing of stock counting, although this will be relatively unimportant cumulatively.
Or, since the data discrepancy coincides with the introduction of the single European market it may be a statistical black hole.
Despite these reservations, however, the WBMS believes analysis points to potentially significant stocks of refeined copper in the Netherland previously not reported.
